BERLIN — A Berlin-based search engine used by government services is dropping its French AI partner, Mistral, in favor of open-source models, including those from China, its CEO told POLITICO.

“We are disappointed with the quality of Mistral,” Ecosia founder and CEO Christian Kroll said in an interview, stating that the models from France’s flagship AI lab are now “a year behind” the competition.

Ecosia — a German web browser and search engine that has built its brand on support for climate action and independence from non-European tech — is used by institutions ranging from Germany’s federal environment ministry to the U.K.’s National Health Service.

In May, it replaced the American giant OpenAI with Mistral as its AI provider. But the company experienced recurring technical problems, including overloaded servers, Kroll said. “We were simply too large a customer for Mistral,” Kroll said

Ecosia also has concerns about whether Mistral aligns with its environmental goals, given the large share of nuclear power in France’s energy mix and questions whether it guarantees European independence. “The fact that Mistral relies on investment from international investors is, in our view, not truly sovereign,” Kroll said.

Mistral did not respond to a request to comment for this article. However, Guillaume Lample, chief scientist and co-founder of Mistral, told POLITICO at a press conference Monday: “I would encourage them to test our new model as soon as possible. We can even give them early access today if they want.”

“And really, the idea here is that it takes time to build great models. It takes computing power, it takes science, and we truly believe we’re growing exponentially. So I encourage them to ride that exponential growth with us, but also to take advantage of our comprehensive customization approach. We can provide customers with the weights of our various models — the large ones, but also the smaller ones — and we can customize them together with them,” Lample said.

Mistral on Tuesday released a new model, Large 4, which far-right National Rally President Jordan Bardella said “puts France (and Europe) back in the race for artificial intelligence.”

With Mistral the clear frontrunner for AI in Europe, Ecosia’s switch raises questions about the bloc’s top company and illustrates the scale of the challenge of building a competitive, sovereign AI model on European soil. Mistral has raised billions of euros from investors abroad, including South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and American giant Nvidia.

Kroll said he sees open-weight models, championed by China, as a huge opportunity for Europe. While the continent missed the first phase of the generative AI boom, the German entrepreneur said Europe can build on increasingly powerful open-source models without investing billions in training frontier systems.

That mirrors an approach being backed by EU leaders and advisors as they seek to reorient the bloc’s AI strategy.

To that end, Ecosia is partnering with the AI platform Melious, which hosts a range of open-source and open-weight models, including Chinese models Qwen, GLM, and Kimi. “We've roughly cut our costs in half while improving quality and performance,“ Kroll said.

Amid strong U.S. concerns about the national security implications of Chinese models, Western research organizations have also raised concerns about the models’ effectiveness given their censorship on politically sensitive topics. A recent NewsGuard investigation found the five leading Chinese-backed AI models repeatedly failed to correct pro-China falsehoods.

But Kroll said such biases are not a dealbreaker, arguing that geopolitical distortions can be addressed through technical measures — unlike shortcomings in model quality.

That’s disputed by some experts. “Overt censorship — that is, refusals to answer or evasive answers ... can be largely eliminated through targeted retraining. This is well-documented technically and is already being done in practice,” said Rasmus Rothe, executive director of the German AI Association.

Subtle bias is more difficult to address, “because it’s embedded in the training data and in what the model takes for granted. With a few hundred example questions, you can scratch the surface, but you won’t reach the foundation,” Rothe said.

DUBLIN — The Irish capital, which doubles as Europe's de facto tech capital, hosted two very different AI summits in the past week.

Most eyes were on the International AI Summit , the signature tech event of Ireland's six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, where top brass from the world's biggest tech firms discussed ways to harness artificial intelligence and minimize safety risks.

But the weekend before, a very different conversation was taking place at the Workers' AI Counter Summit , as Ireland's tech workers demanded a say in how the burgeoning technology reshapes the workplace and society.

Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

### Rise in layoffs

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

“The tech industry was founded on the idea that it would never have a union, because they're making people rich, and treat them really well,” Bohan said. “But post-Covid, workforce adjustments happened again and again, with layoffs and declining conditions in the sector. We started to see more people wanting to get organized around redundancies.”

The spike in sign-ups coincides with a wave of layoffs in Ireland’s tech bubble (and the tech sector globally ), as companies corrected pandemic-era overhiring, and diverted investment to AI.

Ireland hosts the EU headquarters of most of the world’s largest tech companies, and more than 170,000 people are employed in the tech sector, according to the country's statistics institute.

Social media giant Meta has roughly halved its workforce in Ireland since the pandemic, axing well over 1,000 roles to offset AI investment and boost efficiency. Separately, Meta subcontractor Covalen also announced massive layoffs earlier this year, cutting more than 700 people.

Video-sharing platform TikTok announced this year it would shed around 300 Irish jobs , mostly from its trust and safety team, shifting the work to other countries, outsourced vendors or automated AI solutions.

A report by the IMF earlier this year warned that Ireland’s labor market is “relatively more exposed” to AI than many advanced economies, partly due to its concentration of tech workers.

The AI race is also creating new jobs on the Irish market – as AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI are setting up Irish bases and trying to lure Big Tech workers with even bigger salaries.

Amid the uncertainty and volatility of the AI boom, tech workers are turning to unions for the first time as a safety net. One tech worker who used to work in trust and safety at a big tech firm told POLITICO that there used to be a feeling that as a “pampered” tech worker you “can't ask for your rights, because you already have it so much better."

But as layoffs continue and teams get leaner, workers in fields like trust and safety “now have to deal with these issues with fewer and fewer resources”, and face a “constant threat of being chopped,” the worker said.

That’s causing an “undoing of a certain perspective that we have of ourselves as tech sector workers,” they said, “because of undeniable experiences that now put us in situations where we clearly see our rights being violated, even if we may have it so much or somewhat better than most people."

A different tech worker who currently works for Covalen told POLITICO that there is a sense that “if they believe they can replace you with AI, they will do that.”

“All these Big Tech firms only care about profit, and what I have realized is the Irish government protects that Big Tech capital [rather than workers]," the Covalen worker said. "But the question is, what’s the government going to do when the tech bros change their mind and move elsewhere?”

### Workers at the center

The speaker list at this week’s AI summit was a flex of the country’s strength as a tech hub, as top names from the world’s biggest companies like Google and Microsoft took to the stage.

Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, head of organizing and campaigning at Ireland’s Communications Workers’ Union (DATA’s parent union), was the only union voice on the line-up.

"The fact that 36 executives and industry bosses featured on the program, compared with just one trade union speaker — invited at the last minute after attention was drawn to the absence of workers’ voices — says a lot about the value the Irish government places on AI’s impact on workers," she told POLITICO.

"The reality is that a meaningful conversation about AI’s future can only happen through genuine engagement with workers and collective bargaining," Ní Bhrógáin added. "Without that voice, we risk deepening mistrust and resistance rather than creating the conditions for workers to shape these changes collectively." DATA organized its counter-AI summit the previous weekend, to put “workers at the center of the debate about power, AI, technology and the future of work.”

The event cut through the “hype and futurism of politicians and industry figures to focus on the real present harms faced by ordinary workers and communities,” DATA's Bohan said.

The union is pushing for stronger legal protections for tech workers caught up in AI-driven layoffs in Ireland, including making it mandatory for employers to recognize unions during collective bargaining. It is also calling for a ban on cooling-off clauses that prevent laid-off workers from moving between Big Tech subcontractors.

A spokesperson for Ireland’s department for enterprise told POLITICO in a written statement that the government is “committed to strengthening collective bargaining and industrial relations” and has published an action plan to do so between now and 2030.

They said that employers already have to comply with obligations under Irish employment law, including consultation and notification procedures for collective redundancies, and workers who feel those rules have been broken can complain to the Workplace Relations Commission.

### Firefighting to future-proofing

Naoise Ó Cearúil, a center-right Fianna Fáil lawmaker who chairs the AI committee, pointed out that while there have been high-profile job cuts in Ireland’s tech sector, “the actual net is that there has been an increase [in jobs], particularly over the past year and even five years.”

According to Ireland’s central statistics office, total employment in tech and related sectors surpassed 177,000 in the second quarter of this year, up from around 144,000 at the same time in 2021.

Ó Cearúil pointed out that many job losses were in trust and safety jobs like content moderation that are “very difficult mentally,” and now tech firms are able to “utilize AI and software to be able to do a lot of detection, rather than using humans.”

He has called for a national program to be established, to support workers whose jobs are at risk due to AI and automation.

A spokesperson for Ireland’s department of enterprise acknowledged that the country’s tech sector has “experienced significant adjustment in recent years,” but said the changes were generally part of wider global restructuring “rather than reflecting any Ireland-specific weakness.”

They said the Irish government is currently focused on “ensuring workers and businesses are equipped to adapt to technological change through investment in education, training, lifelong learning and digital skills."
